The show is a fizzy delight that succeeds in translating Disney'
Disney's 'Newsies' turns out to be a surprisingly vigorous and well-crafted musical that succeeds in spite of its corporate origins.
There's not much news in "Newsies," but its most appealing headlines are selling hunks and hope.
The great asset of "Newsies," a show that should not be underestimated in its potential trajectory, is a demonstrable comfort in its own emotional skin and theatrical limitations.
Unfortunately, that is not the same as being exciting.

Newsies, which opened Thursday night on Broadway, is great fun, a rock-'em sock-'em American musical with all the trimmings, and an electrifying display that says, yes, formulas make sense when real artists make them work.
Like Oliver! and Annie before it, Newsies delivers the news that on Broadway, orphans can be irresistible.
The show has since been tweaked and polished to a dazzling family friendly delight; and if not "King Of New York," I have to say it's loaded with some very appealing princes.
“Newsies” gets syrupy faster than I hoped for and while never less than assured, its efforts to earn applause can come mighty close to pandering.

Newsies' contrivances are served with a light, knowing touch, and made even more palatable by the easy infectiousness of Alan Menken and Jack Feldman's songs and the youthful exuberance of the cast, under Jeff Calhoun's sprightly direction.
But unlike his earlier hits, this production never really succeeds in carrying us to the height of emotion.
Theatrical Production stage version is a cheerfully old-fashioned mix of a stirring story with a catchy score.
At a time when trade unions are beaten down by the big-money people who run our country, it is thrilling to see a play that celebrates the struggle of workers to get decent pay.

cn.t: Critics praise this energetic Disney musical's dazzling choreography and catchy Menken score, calling it old-fashioned family entertainment. A few find it overly simplistic, but most celebrate its spirited, crowd-pleasing appeal.

sg.ra: The Nederlander is a relatively compact 1,232-seat 1921 Walter C. Jordan house (architect William Neil Smith) with a shallow orchestra rake, so you want to sit forward of where the problems begin; center rows B-E sit forward of the mezz overhang (which becomes notable at row M) and forward of where the shallow rake starts costing shorter patrons their sightlines, giving a direct center look at the 86-ft-wide stage.

sg.vl: Smart value under the overhang line
sg.ra: The Nederlander mezz overhang is 'notable by row M and cuts into the stage at row Q,' so center rows L-O sit just on the safe side of that line - you get a sub-premium price in a 1921 house known historically for being overlooked on its lone 41st Street block (the southernmost Broadway theater), without the shallow-rake head-blocking that plagues the back half.

sg.vl: Where the overhang eats the stage
sg.ra: This is the Nederlander-specific trap: the mezz overhang 'cuts into the stage at row Q,' and the 1921 orchestra's shallow rake means a tall patron in front of you is a real problem - one Redwood patron reported the overhang 'cuts off about the top 20% of the stage,' which mattered because that show featured climbing a redwood; skip for anything with vertical staging or flying effects.

The Nederlander's mezz is raked steeply enough that sightlines stay clean even though you're in a 1921 house without an elevator - rows BB and CC beat row AA because AA has a safety bar across the front that 'may be too high for shorter theatergoers' and 'can cut into the stage'; the center front mezz here looks down into the 40-ft proscenium cleanly.

Multiple guides single out the last two front-mezz rows (DD, EE) as the best 'value for money' at the Nederlander - you're still in the front mezz bloc with the steep mezz rake that keeps the 1921 house's sightlines clean, but priced below rows AA-CC; the tradeoff is legroom which is tight across the mezz here.

The Nederlander has no balcony - the rear mezz is the top tier - and the house is a compact 1,232 seats, so even the 'farthest' seat isn't far; the mezz rake stays steep enough that middle seats FF-JJ hold up, and this is the southernmost Broadway theater (208 W 41st, unusually isolated from the 44th-45th Street cluster), which typically keeps these prices lower than comparable rear-mezz at flagship houses.

sg.vl: Last rows of a no-elevator house
sg.ra: The Nederlander has 'no elevators or escalators' - a 1921 house quirk that matters when you're climbing to rows KK-PP - and a Tripadvisor thread flagged that row JJ sits above a stairwell entryway with a railing bar that can intrude; beyond JJ you're in the last stretch of a 10-row rear mezz (FF-PP) with tight legroom and the most angled sightlines in the house, and this is the top tier since there's no balcony.
